newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zaire force seen only as short-term palliative.
newsitem.headline: Zaire force seen only as short-term palliative.

text.p: The planned international peace force for eastern Zaire, which is likely to see South Africa contribute to such an operation for the first time, can provide only a short-term palliative, military analysts said.
"It's only a first step, not a solution," said Bill Sass, a retired South African defence force brigadier who does research for the independent Institute for Defence Policy think tank.
"The sooner you intervene militarily in a situation like Zaire, the more chance you have of success. But in the long term, I'm not sure how you get back a semblance of normality there."
Sass said the risks for the international forces involved were not as great in Zaire as they had been in Somalia, where U.S. and other foreign troops failed to impose order on feuding warlords.
"In Zaire, Rwanda and Burundi at least there's someone you can negotiate with, someone who's supposed to be in control. But if nothing is done there, it could develop into another Somalia."
President Nelson Mandela has sent an envoy to Tanzania to assess how best South Africa can contribute to the Canadian-led peace operation.
Sass said one of the most important considerations was who would pick up the tab, because South Africa had no extra money for such an operation.
But he said South Africa had no choice but to take part if it wanted to take its rightful post-apartheid place in African affairs.
South African troops regularly raided neighbouring countries in the apartheid years and fought for more than decade in southern Angola against black liberation guerrillas and Cuban forces.

Russell Travers, a senior adviser in the U.S. Defence Intelligence Agency, said more and more multilateral peace operations were likely as the trend towards "smaller, messier" wars like the one in eastern Zaire grew.
"We're going to see more and more of these things, and in many cases they're just not amenable to military solutions," he said.

"If we want to deal with these problems it's going to require us to deal with the long-term systemic problems that many of these areas have and unfortunately the world's not doing too well at this point."
Travers was addressing a symposium at South Africa's two- yearly defence exhibition, which is showcasing the country's home-grown arms and its modifications to foreign systems.
South African mine-clearing equipment has been bought by Britain for use by its peacekeeping forces in Bosnia.
Travers said there were severe limitations to the ability of the military to deal with many of today's problems.
"If the political will is there and military force can be deployed early, it can serve as a deterrent...
"But in terms of ability to alleviate suffering, that isn't a military problem and that's something the world is going to have to focus on...
"Otherwise the military is going to be called on to work some of these problems and I think we're going to find a force-mission mismatch," Travers said.
He said defence planners in the United States and other powers were struggling to come to terms with the changing face of global conflict.
"Nobody really has a sense of who the enemy is...the enemy is uncertainty. We in the United States are struggling with what the precise missions are supposed to be of our military in the future.

"There's lots of very fundamental questions that are just unresolved...The trend over the last several years and the trend into the future will be to defer the hardest decisions, because that is the easiest approach to take, and I suspect it's going to come back and haunt many of us," Travers said.
